data.long_meaning: Baruna is a name derived from Sanskrit, meaning the goddess of oceans and rivers. In Hindu mythology, Baruna is the wife of Devanagri God, Revanta, and is the mother of Yama, the God of death. Baruna is also revered as the goddess of fertility and nourishment. The name Baruna carries the meaning “Goddess of oceans and rivers” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Baruna usually hope their child will grow to embody goddess of oceans and rivers and live with faith, good character and purpose.

data.cultural_impact: Baruna is an evocative Sanskrit name that invokes the rich cultural heritage of ancient India. It is a name synonymous with water bodies, putting the mind at ease, reminding us of the calm and soothing effects of water. The name is deeply embedded in Indian folklore, tradition, and art, and is often used in religious and cultural contexts, especially during auspicious events and celebrations.
data.spiritual_significance: Baruna embodies the spiritual essence of nourishment, fertility, and sustenance. Water represents the divine mother or Shakti, the life-giving force that sustains all forms of life. data.spiritual_symbolism: Baruna is the goddess of the monsoon season and the goddess of fertility and abundance. She is often depicted holding a lotus or a conch shell, and is known to bring prosperity and blessings to her devotees.

historical_references.reference: Baruna is mentioned in the Rigveda, one of the oldest existing texts in the Hindu religion, composed around 1500-1200 BCE. She is described as the goddess of rivers and oceans, often invoked during rituals for abundant rainfall and prosperity.

Baruna is also identified with Saraswati, the goddess of knowledge and wisdom, in the Hindu Puranas, texts that depict ancient Indian history, mythology, and philosophy. She is believed to have bestowed the Vedas, the sacred scriptures of Hinduism, upon the sage Vyasa.
